extracted.intended_audience: educated readers, naturalists, and philosophers interested in human evolution and moral psychology
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarising Darwin's criteria and principles about how intellectual and moral faculties (sympathy, conscience, social instincts, etc.) arise and are modified by natural selection, habit, imitation, and civilisation. Focuses on mechanisms, selective contexts (within-tribe vs between-tribe), and civilisational effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher versus lower moral rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The higher moral rules are founded on the social instincts and relate to the welfare of others; they are supported by the approbation of our fellow-men and by reason. The lower rules relate chiefly to self, arise from public opinion matured by experience and cultivation, and are not practised by rude tribes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher rules: altruistic, socially oriented, reinforced by social approbation and rational reflection. Lower rules: self-regarding, emergent from public opinion and habit, often absent in less civilised peoples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of sympathy with civilisation
rubrics_metrics.description: As man advances in civilisation, social instincts and sympathies extend from family to tribe, to nation, and (potentially) to all men and races; only artificial barriers (differences of appearance or habits) prevent wider sympathy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sympathy expansion is gradual and culturally mediated; differences in appearance/habit can retard extension. Examples: Romans' gladiatorial exhibitions and Gauchos' unfamiliarity with 'humanity' illustrate limited sympathy in some cultures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanity to lower animals as late moral acquisition
rubrics_metrics.description: Sympathy beyond the confines of man (humanity to lower animals) is one of the latest moral acquisitions and is generally absent in savages except toward pets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This virtue arises incidentally from more tender and widely diffused sympathies; once practised by some, it spreads through instruction and example and is incorporated into public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of thoughts as highest moral stage
rubrics_metrics.description: The highest stage of moral culture is the power to control one's thoughts and not even to think again on past sins; habitual thoughts dye the soul and familiarization with bad actions makes their performance easier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral education should aim at shaping habitual thoughts; literary quotation (Tennyson, Marcus Aurelius) supports idea that internal mental discipline is central to character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible inheritance of moral tendencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtuous or vicious tendencies may be inherited to some degree; experiences of utility consolidated over generations could produce faculties of moral intuition not based on individual experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin notes anecdotal family tendencies (stealing, lying) and links moral tendencies to bodily/brain state and to hereditary mental derangement; but he expresses caution and doubt about transmission of senseless customs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habit, instruction and example codify virtues across generations
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtues like chastity, temperance, and humanity to animals may first be impressed on mental organisation through habit, instruction and example continued during several generations in the same family, with inheritance playing a subordinate role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural transmission (habit and pedagogy) is emphasised as primary; natural selection via individual reproductive advantage is not necessarily the main route for such traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social instincts as basis of rudimentary moral rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Social instincts acquired for communal good yield early impulses to aid fellows and to heed approbation and disapprobation; these provide a rudimentary rule of right and wrong which is refined with intellect and habit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social instincts likely evolved by natural selection and serve as the seed for more complex morality shaped by reason, religion, and instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural selection's role in perfecting intellectual faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: Intellectual faculties that aided survival (inventing tools, adapting habits, division of labour) would have been perfected through natural selection because tribes with more such individuals tended to increase and supplant others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Success of tribes depends largely on arts and intellect; even small advantages in sagacity would be amplified by imitation and tribe-level demographic success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation as mechanism for spreading inventions and strengthening intellect
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of imitation (together with reason and experience) increases and modifies intellectual powers: when one individual invents a useful tool or practice, others imitate and benefit, reinforcing cognitive development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence from apes and savages shows imitation and learning by experience; habitual practice of arts slightly strengthens intellect and increases chances of further innovation in tribes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group-level selection of social and moral qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: When tribes compete, those with larger numbers of courageous, sympathetic and faithful members (ready to aid each other) gain advantage and supplant other tribes; thus social and moral qualities can be advanced by natural selection at the group level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin marshals examples of tribal warfare and advantages of discipline/obedience; group success—not individual reproductive advantage within a tribe—is the selective context here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of within-tribe natural selection on altruism
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the same tribe, traits like extreme courage or self-sacrifice may not be increased by selection because such individuals often perish or leave fewer offspring; hence individual-level selection within tribes may not favor high altruism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin argues that the bravest may die more often, so mechanisms other than differential reproduction must account for spread of altruistic behavior within tribes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habit, reciprocity, and social approbation as drivers of internal moralisation
rubrics_metrics.description: As reasoning and foresight improve, individuals learn that aiding others yields reciprocal aid; praise and blame of fellow-men (love of glory, fear of shame) induce habits of benevolence and strengthen sympathy into durable moral sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise/blame and the sentiment of glory are powerful stimuli; even dogs and savages show appreciation of encouragement and shame, indicating early moral psychology rooted in social feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason and foresight produce self-regarding virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: With increased experience and reasoning humans perceive remote consequences of actions and thus value self-regarding virtues (temperance, chastity) that were disregarded in earlier times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-regarding virtues grow through intellectual understanding of future effects, habit, and social approval; Darwin refers back to chapter on development of such virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscience as complex sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Conscience emerges as a complex sentiment originating in social instincts and guided by approbation, reason, self-interest, religion, instruction, and habit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral sense is composite and evolves in sophistication as societies and individual cognition advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civilisation reduces natural elimination of the weak
rubrics_metrics.description: Civilised societies check the elimination of the weak (build asylums, poor-laws, medical interventions such as vaccination), allowing the weak in body or mind to survive and propagate, which may be injurious to the race if unchecked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin notes the tension between moral impulse to aid the helpless and potential long-term biological consequences; he also mentions that complete neglect of the weak would be morally unacceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensatory checks on degeneration in civilisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Various checks mitigate the potential degenerative effects of civilisation: weaker individuals marry less freely; conscription removes fitter men (reducing their reproductive success); inheritance and social structures influence reproductive patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin enumerates mechanisms (reduced marriage of weak, conscription, inheritance timing, primogeniture, marrying heiresses) that complicate simple predictions about degeneration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of wealth and property on selection and progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Accumulation and inheritance of property give children of the rich advantages independent of bodily or mental superiority, but moderate wealth does not necessarily impede selection because able individuals still succeed in trades and professions; extreme wealth can create 'drones' but their numbers are small and other checks operate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin sees both positive and negative effects of wealth: necessary for arts and progress but also potentially insulating unfit individuals; social dynamics (marriage patterns) complicate outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civilisation's net effect on physical and intellectual development
rubrics_metrics.description: Civilisation tends to favour better bodily development through better food and relief from hardships (civilised peoples often physically stronger than savages); for intellect, there can be a tendency for increase because intellectually superior members often succeed and have more offspring, though this may be counterbalanced by other factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical observations (comparative strength, longevity tables) suggest civilisation can improve body and possibly intellect, but the net genetic consequences are complex.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cumulative selection vs preservation of rare anomalies in intellectual progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Advancement of species (and intellectual faculties) arises mainly from selection of slight, heritable improvements and elimination of slightly inferior individuals, not from preserving rare prodigies; therefore prodigies who leave no offspring may still advance mankind culturally without contributing genetically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy with domesticated animals: breeding from slightly better individuals shifts the average; cultural achievements of geniuses contribute to progress even if they don't reproduce.
